title: Order and customer audit
prompt: The data team audits orders against customers, and must see both sides of every mismatch. Write `solve(orders, customers)` so it returns every order and every customer, matched where they can be.
rules: `order_customer` is the order's own `customer_id`; `customer_id` is the id from `customers`. An order matches a customer with the same id, and a missing id never matches anything, not even another missing id.
An order with no match has `customer_id` and `name` missing. A customer with no orders has `order_id` and `order_customer` missing.
If `customers` lists the same id twice, its orders appear once per listing, so the audit shows the duplicate. Return `order_id`, `order_customer`, `customer_id` and `name`, in that order.
hints: Both sides must be kept whole, so this is a full join.

With `on="customer_id"` there's only one key column, filled from whichever side has it, and you can't tell the sides apart. Join on a condition instead: `orders["customer_id"] == customers["customer_id"]`.
With a condition both key columns are kept. Pick each one with `orders["customer_id"]` or `customers["customer_id"]` and rename it with `.alias(...)`.
explanation: This is a full join on a condition, so both key columns survive: `orders.join(customers, orders["customer_id"] == customers["customer_id"], "full")`, then `select("order_id", orders["customer_id"].alias("order_customer"), customers["customer_id"].alias("customer_id"), "name")`. A NULL key compares as NULL, never true, so an order with no customer id and a customer with no id each appear on their own row. A customer listed twice matches each of its orders twice, which is what an audit should expose. Joining with `on="customer_id"` gives one merged key column, so an orphan order and a customer with no orders look alike.
